dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ktorý byt je lepší?
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a room to rent. Eva helps him compare two options on her phone screen.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Pozri, tento byt je väčší, ale drahší.
lines.id: Look, this apartment is bigger, but more expensive.
lines.literal: look, this apartment is bigger, but more-expensive.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: O sto eur mesačne. Ale je bližšie k centru.

notes: **Väčší, menší, lepší, krajší** — four irregular comparatives, and all four are among the most frequently used in the language. Their base forms (*veľký, malý, dobrý, pekný*) can't be seen in them at all. Learn them in pairs from now on.

**O koľko drahší?** — the difference is expressed with *o* + accusative: *o sto eur* (a hundred euros more), *o dva roky starší* (two years older), *o hodinu neskôr* (an hour later). A very useful and easy pattern.

**Rýchlejšie ako odtiaľto** — the thing you compare with is introduced by *ako* (or *než*, which is slightly more formal). The word after it stays in its basic form: *väčší ako ja*, not *väčší ako mňa*.
**Najdôležitejší, najlepšia** — the superlative is formed by putting *naj-* in front of the comparative. One prefix, the whole system. This is one of the cheapest parts of all Slovak grammar.

**Bližšie and rýchlejšie are adverbs, not adjectives.** Notice the ending *-ie*, not *-í*. *Je bližší* (it is closer — a quality of the thing) but *Je bližšie* (it's located closer — an adverb). The difference is slight and beginners often ignore it.

grammars.title: Comparative and superlative
body: The comparative is formed with the ending **-ší** or **-ejší**. The superlative is formed by adding the prefix **naj-** to the comparative. There is no third step.
after: **When -ší and when -ejší?** Short adjectives whose stem ends in one consonant take **-ší** (*starší, mladší, dlhší*). Adjectives whose stem ends in two consonants take **-ejší** (*lacnejší, rýchlejší*), because three consonants in a row are hard to pronounce. If in doubt, use *-ejší* — it's right more often.

**The ending still changes with gender**, like any adjective: *starší brat* (m), *staršia sestra* (f), *staršie mesto* (n), *starší ľudia* (masculine plural). You're not learning a new system, just attaching it to a longer stem.

**Five irregular ones, and all five must be learned:** *veľký → **väčší***, *malý → **menší***, *dobrý → **lepší***, *zlý → **horší***, *pekný/krásny → **krajší***. All five are among the most common adjectives — so learning them now is far cheaper than repeating the mistakes later.

grammars.title: The rhythm rule, up close
body: Adjective endings are the best place to watch the rhythm rule at work, because here you see it on the same word, side by side.
after: **What counts as long**: vowels with an accent mark (*á é í ó ú ý*), diphthongs (*ia ie iu*), *ô*, and *ŕ ĺ*. Look at the fourth row: *biely* has a short ending because *ie* is a diphthong, and diphthongs count as long even without a mark.

**The comparative almost always takes a short ending**, because its stem already contains a long syllable: *krajší* (not *krajšý*), *staršia* (not *staršiá*), *najlepšie*. You practically don't need to think about it here.

**If you write a long ending where it should be short**, your sentence reads as Czech, not as an ordinary mistake. Czech has no rhythm rule and writes *krásná*. Slovaks hear the difference immediately.

blocks.text: Notice that **starý** appears twice — it's the opposite of *nový* (for things) and of *mladý* (for people). Slovak, just like English with *old*, uses one word for both.

Colors behave exactly like other adjectives: *biely dom* (m), *biela káva* (f), *biele auto* (n). Notice that *biely* and *čierny* take a short ending because the stem is long — *bie-* is a diphthong, *čier-* is a diphthong. The rhythm rule again.

blocks.text: **Ako and než mean the same thing**, and both are correct. *Ako* is heard more in conversation; *než* is slightly more formal and more common in writing. Pick one and stick with it.
